candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.9999 malware probability, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking (SHAP +0.006300 to +0.016850). However, the evidence itself is weak. Every n-gram has a relative frequency of 0.000000, and no function locations, API references, constants or strings are listed, so none of the patterns can be tied to a specific routine such as a hashing loop. All 20 are short, generic two-instruction sequences that appear in ordinary compiled code: call/return scaffolding (XOR CALL, CALL ADD, LEA CALL, CALL XOR, PUSH SUB, ADD POP), flag-test branches (TEST JZ, TEST JS, MOV JZ, CMP JL) and register/stack arithmetic (SUB MOV, SUB LEA, MOV LEA, AND MOV, XOR MOV). A few are modestly suggestive of bitwise mixing or branchless conditional logic: XOR XOR (+0.008826), XOR SHL (+0.007046), XOR CMOVNZ (+0.007577), CMOVZ MOV (+0.016850, the top-ranked feature) and CMP CMOVZ (+0.006956). Such logic can occur in hash or cipher inner loops, but it also appears in compiler-optimized non-mining code. The SHAP contributions are spread fairly evenly (no single feature above 0.017), which suggests a diffuse statistical signature rather than one decisive indicator. The model's score indicates the binary resembles known malicious samples in its training data, but this evidence does not independently show mining behavior. The result is suspicious but inconclusive on cryptojacking specifically.
